title: The first aorist

objectives.can: Recognise first-aorist active and middle indicatives and parse them.

explanation.summary: The aorist is the tense-form that presents an action as a whole, without looking inside it. In the indicative it is the ordinary way to tell what happened. The first aorist adds -σα- to the stem and takes an augment.

sections.heading: What the aorist does
body: Greek verbs do not only say when something happens. They also say how the speaker looks at it. The present and the imperfect usually look inside an action, as in progress or as repeated. The aorist looks at the action from outside and presents it as a whole, a complete event, whether that event was short or long.

So the aorist is not 'once for all' and not a 'point' in time. John writes ἠγάπησεν, 'he loved', and the aorist does not say whether that love lasted a moment or an age; it simply presents the act as a whole. In the indicative the augment marks the action as past, so an aorist indicative is usually translated with an English past tense. English cannot always show the difference from the imperfect, and you will often see only the context.

sections.heading: Augment, stem and -σα-
body: A first-aorist active is built in three parts: an augment, the verbal stem, and the tense sign σα with the endings -α, -ας, -ε(ν), -αμεν, -ατε, -αν. From πιστεύω, ἐπίστευσα is ἐ- (augment) + πιστευ- (stem) + -σα. The augment is the same one you met in the imperfect: ἐ- before a consonant, a lengthened vowel before a vowel (ἀκούω gives ἤκουσα), and between a prefix and the stem in a compound (ἀποστέλλω gives ἀπέστειλα).

What separates the aorist from the imperfect of the same verb is the σ after the stem (or the change of stem it brings), and the endings -α, -αμεν, -ατε, -αν instead of the imperfect's -ον, -ομεν, -ετε, -ον. Compare ἐποίησεν, aorist, with the imperfect ἐποίει.

sections.heading: When the σ hides or goes
body: Before σ, stem consonants change as they did in the future. Labial stops (π, β, φ) and σ make ψ: γράφω gives ἔγραψα and πέμπω gives ἔπεμψα. Velar stops (κ, γ, χ, and the σσ of κηρύσσω) make ξ: ἐκήρυξεν. Dental stops (τ, δ, θ) and ζ drop out before σ: βαπτίζω gives ἐβάπτισα, δοξάζω gives ἐδόξασα, σῴζω gives ἔσωσεν.
Contract verbs lengthen their final stem vowel: ποιέω gives ἐποίησα, λαλέω gives ἐλάλησα, ἀγαπάω gives ἠγάπησα. A few keep the vowel short; καλέω has ἐκάλεσεν.

Verbs whose stem ends in λ, μ, ν or ρ (liquid verbs) usually have no σ at all. They lengthen the stem vowel instead and take the same endings: μένω has ἔμεινεν, κρίνω has ἔκρινα, ἀποστέλλω has ἀπέστειλα, ἐγείρω has ἤγειρεν.

sections.heading: The middle
body: The first-aorist middle has the same stem and tense sign as the active, with the middle endings: -σάμην, -σω, -σατο, -σάμεθα, -σασθε, -σαντο. A middle often shows that the subject acts on, for or with reference to itself: the middle ἐποιησάμην in Acts 1:1 has the author as the one who composed his own account. Many verbs, however, simply have middle forms with an active meaning, and you learn them that way: ἀπεκρίνατο ('he answered'), ἤρξατο ('he began'), ἐξελέξατο ('he chose').

misunderstandings: The aorist does not mean 'once for all', 'momentary' or 'single'. It presents an action as a whole; the action itself may have been long, repeated or abstract.
The augment does not by itself make a verb aorist. The imperfect has it too. Look for the σ (or ψ, ξ), or for the changed stem of a liquid verb, and for the endings -α, -αμεν, -ατε, -αν.
The first-aorist ending -α looks like the ending of the perfect (ἔγραψα, but γέγραφα). The perfect has reduplication, not an augment, and a κ in many verbs (next lessons).
A middle ending is not always a reflexive meaning. ἀπεκρίνατο means 'he answered', not 'he answered himself'.

deeper.heading: Why 'first' aorist?
body: Handbooks call it the 'first' aorist because it is the regular type, formed with σα on the stem. The 'second' aorist is a different formation of the same tense-form: it has a changed stem and the endings of the imperfect. Both are the aorist: they present the action in the same way and differ only in how the forms are built, so they are best learned together as one tense-form with two shapes.
